references.text: The sacrifice animal was to be brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, and the hand was to be laid on the animal's head, the same ritual as described for the burnt offering.
Laying hands on the head of the sacrifice animal and slaughtering at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, an identical ritual for the peace offering.
Moses brought forward the sin offering bull, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the bull's head, the same procedure during the consecration of priests.
On the Day of Atonement, Aaron was to lay both hands on the goat's head; the laying on of hands symbolizes the transfer of sin.
During the consecration of priests, the bull was to be brought forward before the Tent of Meeting, and Aaron and his sons were to lay their hands on the bull's head.
The Levites were to lay their hands on the heads of the bulls; the laying on of hands as part of the cleansing ritual.
Christ entered the holy place with his own blood, not with the blood of goats and calves, and completed the sacrifice that the sin offering in Leviticus pointed toward.
The blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sins, showing that the sin offering in 3. Mosebok was a shadow of the perfect sacrifice in Christ.
Confirms that slaughter must always take place at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting as a constant liturgical norm.
Demonstrates that the laying on of hands as a symbol of transferring guilt is identical whether the offering is brought by an individual or by elders.
Confirms that ritual requirements for laying on of hands and slaughter apply regardless of whether the sacrifice animal is a bull or a goat.
An explicit reference confirming that the ritual standard for bull blood (sin offering) also applies to the people's sin offering goat.
Continues the same ritual action from slaughter (v.4) to the application of blood on the altar.
Confirms that the ritual standard for slaughter is universal for all types of sin offerings, regardless of the value of the offering.
